Specific course details (such as prerequisites, course seminar, format, learning outcomes, assessment methods, and resource needs) will be determined by the faculty member(s) who propose a specific seminar course in this area. Consider this worked case: An instructor might choose a seminar format with three lecture hours per term and assign a research paper as the primary assessment. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.

Specific course instances will be identified as belonging to the Theory cluster, the Security cluster, or both clusters. Consider this worked case: A seminar on secure key management would be classified under both the Theory and Security clusters. On screen, present a Venn diagram with two overlapping circles labeled 'Theory Cluster' and 'Security Cluster', with a course example placed in the intersection. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Contact Hours and make the decision criteria explicit. Security requirements should be tracked throughout development. Consider this worked case: Students attend three weekly sessions, each focusing on a different theoretical or security topic proposed by the faculty. On screen, display a calendar icon with three highlighted blocks labeled 'Lecture 1', 'Lecture 2', and 'Lecture 3' to indicate the required contact hours. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.

beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a calendar icon with three highlighted blocks labeled 'Lecture 1', 'Lecture 2', and 'Lecture 3' to indicate the required contact hours.

beats.narration: Apply Cryptographic Standards Overview to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Cryptographic standards define approved algorithms and parameters. Consider this worked case: The NIST FIPS 197 standard specifies AES encryption parameters, ensuring consistent algorithm usage across systems. On screen, show a document icon with a checklist of approved algorithms and parameters, highlighting 'AES' and 'FIPS 197' as examples. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.

beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a document icon with a checklist of approved algorithms and parameters, highlighting 'AES' and 'FIPS 197' as examples.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Encryption and Confidentiality, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Encryption supports confidentiality when keys and modes are used correctly. Consider this worked case: Using AES in CBC mode with a properly generated 256-bit key ensures that intercepted ciphertext remains unreadable without the key. On screen, illustrate a lock icon with a key turning, showing plaintext transforming into ciphertext, with a note emphasizing correct key and mode usage. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.
beats.title: Encryption and Confidentiality
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Illustrate a lock icon with a key turning, showing plaintext transforming into ciphertext, with a note emphasizing correct key and mode usage.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Integrity and Authenticity Mechanisms with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Message authentication and digital signatures address integrity and authenticity in different ways. Consider this worked case: A digital signature verifies the sender's identity and ensures the message hasn't been altered, while a message authentication code only checks integrity. On screen, display two side-by-side icons: one showing a digital signature with a verified checkmark, and another showing a message authentication tag with an integrity shield. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Integrity and Authenticity Mechanisms
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display two side-by-side icons: one showing a digital signature with a verified checkmark, and another showing a message authentication tag with an integrity shield.

beats.narration: Use Random Number Generation and Key Management to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Random number generation supports keys, nonces, and other security parameters. Consider this worked case: A secure system uses a cryptographically secure random number generator to create unique nonces for each encryption session, and rotates keys quarterly to limit exposure. On screen, show a flowchart with arrows connecting 'Random Number Generation' to 'Key Management', listing each sub-step (generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, revocation, destruction) as nodes. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Random Number Generation and Key Management
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a flowchart with arrows connecting 'Random Number Generation' to 'Key Management', listing each sub-step (generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, revocation, destruction) as nodes.

beats.narration: Connect Secure Software Development Framework to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. The Secure Software Development Framework groups practices into four practice groups. Consider this worked case: Prepare the Organization establishes secure development processes, while Respond to Vulnerabilities identifies and remediates discovered weaknesses. On screen, display a four-quadrant grid, each quadrant labeled with one practice group name, with brief icons representing people/processes (Prepare), code protection (Protect), release/verification (Produce), and vulnerability response (Respond). Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
beats.title: Secure Software Development Framework
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a four-quadrant grid, each quadrant labeled with one practice group name, with brief icons representing people/processes (Prepare), code protection (Protect), release/verification (Produce), and vulnerability response (Respond).

beats.narration: Finish with Verification and Security Reasoning as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Security reasoning identifies assets, trust boundaries, threats, controls, evidence, residual risk, and responsibilities. Consider this worked case: Verification audits the codebase to confirm that encryption standards are applied correctly, while security reasoning maps out system assets and potential threats before development begins. On screen, show a magnifying glass icon over a codebase, with a checklist of verification steps, and a separate diagram showing a network diagram with labeled assets, trust boundaries, and threats. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.

sources.author: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.excerpt: The Secure Software Development Framework groups practices into four practice groups. Prepare the Organization establishes people, processes, and technology for secure development. Protect the Software prevents unauthorized access to code and development artifacts. Produce Well-Secured Software addresses security requirements, design, verification, and release. Respond to Vulnerabilities identifies, analyzes, remediates, and learns from discovered weaknesses. Security requirements should be tracked throughout development. Verification provides evidence that selected practices and controls were performed. Security reasoning identifies assets, trust boundaries, threats, controls, evidence, residual risk, and responsibilities.
sources.title: NIST Secure Software Development Framework

sources.author: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.excerpt: Cryptographic standards define approved algorithms and parameters. Encryption supports confidentiality when keys and modes are used correctly. Message authentication and digital signatures address integrity and authenticity in different ways. Random number generation supports keys, nonces, and other security parameters. Key management covers generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, revocation, and destruction. Modes of operation define how a primitive processes data larger than one block. Validation checks implementations against specified requirements. Security depends on the complete protocol and implementation, not only an algorithm name. Analysis also considers side channels and migration requirements.
